paragraphs.text: Lakeside Campsite — information for visitors. The campsite is open from 1 April to 31 October. Arrivals are between 2 pm and 8 pm, and pitches must be vacated by 11 am on the day of departure. If you expect to arrive after 8 pm, please phone the site office before 6 pm on the day, and a member of staff will leave your welcome pack and a map at the gate.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Each pitch has room for one tent or caravan and one car; additional cars must be left in the overflow car park near the entrance. Electric hook-ups are available on the lower field only and must be booked in advance. Open fires are not permitted anywhere on the site, but raised barbecues may be used on pitches as long as they are kept off the grass.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Quiet hours are from 10.30 pm to 7 am, when music and loud conversation should stop. Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a lead at all times and are not allowed in the shower block or the children’s play area. The site shop sells basic food, gas and firewood for use in the fire pits by the lake, and is open from 8 am to 6 pm.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: Evening talks at the Science Museum — spring series

paragraphs.text: The Hidden Life of Soil (Tuesday 4 March, 7 pm). A soil scientist explains how a single handful of earth contains more organisms than there are people on the planet, and why this matters for farming. The talk includes a short demonstration using microscopes, and a small number of samples will be available to examine afterwards. Suitable for ages 12 and up.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Building the Bridge (Thursday 13 March, 7 pm). An engineer who worked on the new river crossing describes the challenges of building over deep water and the unexpected problems the team encountered. There will be no questions from the floor, but visitors can speak to the speaker informally at a drinks reception afterwards.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Night Skies for Beginners (Tuesday 25 March, 8 pm). An introduction to the constellations visible in spring, followed by a chance to use telescopes in the museum garden if the sky is clear. The talk is free for members; others pay £6. Warm clothing is recommended.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The Chemistry of Cooking (Thursday 3 April, 7 pm). A food scientist explores why bread rises, why onions turn brown and how the temperature of an oven changes taste. Tasting samples are included in the ticket price. Places are limited to forty, and visitors with food allergies should contact the museum before booking.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: C
texts.title: Printing and copying in the office

paragraphs.text: Printing and copying in the office. Multi-function printers, which print, copy and scan, are located in the print room on each floor. All printing is sent to a secure queue: your documents will not be printed until you tap your staff pass on the machine you are using, which means you can collect them from any printer in the building. Documents that have not been collected within twenty-four hours are deleted from the queue automatically. If you print something by mistake, you can delete it from the queue using the touch screen on the printer.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The default settings are double-sided and black and white, and staff are asked not to change these unless there is a good reason. Colour printing costs the company about eight times as much as black and white and should be used only for material going to customers or for charts that cannot be understood without colour. Each department receives a monthly report showing how much it has printed. Printing in colour requires a code that can be obtained from your department manager.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Large jobs of more than 200 pages, and anything that needs binding, laminating or printing on special paper, should be sent to the reprographics team on the ground floor rather than printed on office machines. The team needs two working days’ notice for most jobs and five working days for anything over 1,000 pages.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: If a printer runs out of paper, spare packs are kept in the cupboard in each print room. Toner cartridges must be changed only by the facilities team, who should also be informed of paper jams that cannot be cleared by opening the front panel. Confidential waste paper must be placed in the locked grey bins, not in the ordinary recycling. Any problem that cannot be solved by the facilities team is referred to the printer supplier, who aims to send an engineer within one working day.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: D
texts.title: Working at height: using ladders safely

paragraphs.text: Working at height: using ladders safely. Many accidents at work involve falls from quite low heights, and a large proportion happen while people are using ladders or stepladders for short tasks such as changing a light bulb or reaching a high shelf. Before using a ladder, ask yourself whether the job could be done from the ground or with a safer piece of equipment, such as a platform with handrails. Ladders should be used only for short tasks of no more than thirty minutes.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Only use ladders provided by the company, which are inspected every six months and carry a label showing the date of the last check. Before each use, look for damaged rungs, missing feet or bent sides; if you find a fault, do not use the ladder, and label it as out of use and report it to the facilities team. Never use chairs, desks or boxes to stand on. If you are unsure whether a ladder is safe, ask the facilities team before using it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: When using a leaning ladder, place it on firm, level ground at an angle of about one unit out for every four units up, and make sure the top rests against a solid surface, not against glass or plastic guttering. Keep three points of contact, such as two feet and one hand, at all times, and do not stand on the top three rungs. A second person should hold the foot of any ladder longer than three metres. Do not overreach; move the ladder instead.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Stepladders must be fully opened with the locking bars in place. Do not work from the top step unless it is designed as a platform, and avoid carrying heavy or bulky items while climbing. Anyone who feels unwell or dizzy should not work at height. Staff who use ladders regularly as part of their job must complete the online ladder safety course every two years.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: In many cities the pigeon is so common that it is barely noticed, except as a nuisance. It gathers in squares, nests on window ledges and railway bridges, and feeds on whatever people drop. Yet the bird is not a natural city dweller in the way it might appear. Its ancestor, the rock dove, lived on sea cliffs and in mountain gorges, and the pigeon’s success in urban areas is the result of a long partnership with people that began thousands of years ago and has since been largely forgotten. Understanding that history helps to explain both why pigeons are so common and why efforts to control them so often fail.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The rock dove was one of the first birds to be domesticated. People in the ancient Near East kept doves in towers and specially built dovecotes, collecting the young birds for food and the droppings, which are rich in nitrogen, as fertiliser for their fields. Over centuries, breeding produced birds that nested readily in buildings, reproduced throughout the year rather than only in spring and were comfortable living close to humans. These were the qualities that would later allow escaped and abandoned birds to thrive in cities. Dovecotes were often a sign of wealth, and in some countries the right to keep one was restricted to landowners.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Pigeons also served people in less obvious ways. Their remarkable ability to find their way home over long distances made them valuable messengers, and for centuries they carried news of market prices, the results of races and messages in wartime. Selective breeding produced an extraordinary variety of fancy breeds, with feathered feet, puffed-up chests or unusual tails, and pigeon keeping became a popular hobby in many countries. Some of the earliest studies of inheritance used pigeons, because their many breeds made the effects of selection easy to see. Some messenger birds were even awarded medals for their service, and racing pigeons are still kept by enthusiasts in many countries, where the best birds can be sold for large sums.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: As the use of pigeons for food and messages declined in the twentieth century, many birds were released or escaped, and they found in cities a close copy of the cliffs their ancestors had lived on. Tall buildings offered ledges for nesting, bridges and railway stations gave shelter, and the streets provided a steady supply of food dropped by people or put out deliberately for the birds. Because city pigeons can breed several times a year, their numbers can increase rapidly wherever food is plentiful. In some cities today, estimates put the number of pigeons in the hundreds of thousands, although accurate counts are difficult to make.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The relationship between people and urban pigeons is now an uneasy one. Their droppings damage stonework and can make pavements slippery, and large flocks are unpopular with shop owners and property managers. Pigeons can carry diseases that affect humans, although the risk to most people is considered low. At the same time, many residents enjoy feeding them, and campaigners argue that the birds are part of the life of the city and deserve protection rather than control. Some residents also complain about the noise of large flocks early in the morning, and the conflict between these views is often fought out in local newspapers and council meetings.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Attempts to reduce pigeon numbers by killing them have usually failed. When birds are removed from an area, the remaining birds breed faster and others move in from nearby, so that the population soon returns to its previous level. Research has shown that the size of a pigeon population is determined mainly by the amount of food available, which means that the most effective long-term measure is to reduce feeding. Some cities have banned the feeding of pigeons in public places, with mixed success. Where feeding has been reduced consistently over several years, however, numbers have fallen and stayed low.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Other approaches have been tried. Spikes, nets and wires keep birds off particular buildings but simply move them elsewhere. Several cities have built managed pigeon lofts, where birds are encouraged to nest and some of their eggs are replaced with dummy eggs to limit the number of young. Supporters say such lofts reduce populations gradually and humanely and concentrate droppings in one place where they can be cleaned; critics say they are expensive and have been tested properly in only a few places. Birth-control feed, which reduces the number of eggs laid, has also been tested in some places, and falconers with trained birds of prey have been hired to scare pigeons away from particular sites.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Scientists have recently begun to take a greater interest in city pigeons, not as pests but as subjects of research. Studies have examined how they navigate among tall buildings, how they recognise individual people and how urban populations in different cities are related to one another. The bird that most city dwellers ignore turns out to be a living record of one of humanity’s oldest partnerships with an animal, and of what happens when that partnership comes to an end. Pigeons, it seems, are far more intelligent than their reputation suggests.
paragraphs.label: H
